description: SphereX is a one-person student team from Antalya, Türkiye, working on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. I love astronomy: constellations, stars and discovering new things about our universe. For Space Apps 2026 I built SPHEREx: Sky Detective, a free web game in English and Turkish where players compare SPHEREx-style infrared sky maps over time to find comets, asteroids and a Planet X candidate. Interests: astronomy, games, coding and science education.
summary: SPHEREx: Sky Detective is a free, story-driven web game that answers the challenge's call for a public tool that makes it easy for anyone to see how the sky changes in SPHEREx data. The player becomes a student sky detective helping a science team. In 12 missions, the player drags a PROGRESS bar so a scan beam paints in the next 6-month all-sky map, moves a 102-step wavelength slider modeled on SPHEREx's 102 infrared bands (0.75-5.0 µm), and uses blinking and a magnifier to spot what moved, appeared or faded: comets, asteroids, meteor fragments, brown dwarfs, a supernova and even a Planet X candidate. Each find is identified through a short quiz and unlocks a fact card based on NASA information, a collection card and badges across six rarity tiers. The game runs in any browser with no installation, works offline, and is fully playable in English and Turkish, so classrooms can use it right away. It matters because the methods astronomers use to find moving objects, comparing images over time and across wavelengths, become something students learn by doing.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx: Sky Detective turns the idea behind SPHEREx's repeated all-sky maps into a game anyone can play in a browser. The player is a student sky detective. Every mission opens with a short 3D story cutscene, then the player compares sky fields over time and across infrared wavelengths to find the object that moved, appeared or faded, identifies it, and adds it to a collection.

HOW IT WORKS

1) PROGRESS bar (time): dragging it moves a scan beam across the field; to the left of the beam the sky shows the next 6-month map, mirroring how SPHEREx revisits the whole sky about every six months.

2) Wavelength slider: 102 steps between 0.75 and 5.0 µm, like SPHEREx's 102 bands. Each star's brightness in each band is computed on the GPU from Planck's law, so cool and hot objects really change brightness as the wavelength changes; some targets only show up in specific bands (for example a comet glowing at 4.3 µm, where carbon dioxide emits).

3) Blink comparator and magnifier: switch quickly between two epochs and zoom in to catch small motions.

4) Lock on and identify: clicking the right object draws white lock-on lines, the object takes its rarity color, a "sending data" uplink screen plays, and a short quiz asks what the object is. The correct answer reveals a fact card and the shadowed collection card.

CONTENT

12 story missions, 17 objects (main-belt and near-Earth asteroids, a comet, a brown dwarf, a supernova, broken asteroid fragments, a Kuiper Belt object, Sedna, a Planet X candidate, hypothetical worlds such as Planet Y and Tyche, a primordial black hole candidate, a rogue planet, an interstellar visitor, satellite trails and more), 6 rarity tiers (Common, Rare, Epic, Legendary, Mysterious, Chaotic) and 19 badges. The last chaotic mission adds alien obstacles (static, fake signals, fog) that the player must chase away. An anomaly detector helps with the hardest finds.

NASA SCIENCE BEHIND IT

SPHEREx launched in March 2025, began its survey in May 2025 and completed its first all-sky map in December 2025; it observes in 102 infrared colors from 0.75 to 5.0 µm. SPHEREx's detection of carbon dioxide around interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS inspired the comet mission. The Planet X mission follows NASA's Planet X page: a proposed planet of about 5 to 10 Earth masses that has not been found, so the game labels it a candidate. Public SPHEREx Quick Release data at NASA/IPAC IRSA is the basis for our planned next step.

HONESTY NOTE

The sky fields are simulations built from SPHEREx's real parameters (bands, wavelength range, revisit cadence), not real SPHEREx images. Hypothetical objects are clearly labeled as fictional in the game.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Three.js (r149) and WebGL with custom GLSL shaders (per-band Planck brightness, gravitational lensing); Web Audio API for sound effects; Google Fonts; GitHub Pages hosting. No installation, no account, works offline, runs on school computers. Full English and Turkish interface (TR | EN switch).

CREATIVITY

Instead of a data viewer, the challenge's goal ("make it easy for anyone to see how the sky changes") becomes the core game mechanic: time and wavelength are things the player physically drags, and the collection and rarity system rewards careful looking, the same skill astronomers use.

IMPACT

Students learn how moving and changing objects are actually found (image comparison over time, multi-band imaging, proper motion) by doing it, in their own language. Next steps: a Real Sky mode using public SPHEREx Quick Release images from IRSA, a teacher dashboard and class competitions.

USE OF SI

The game's code and text were written with the help of an SI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) under the team's direction; the story idea, mission design and testing are the team's. Scientific facts were checked against NASA sources. No NASA logos or branding are used in the game.
